X1.name: Brand vs. Single Brand Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from regions with high boat ownership (e.g., Scandinavia). They view a product page for Jotun marine coatings and are asked: (1) "How likely are you to purchase this marine coating for your boat?" (Likert 1‑10). (2) "Which of the following best describes your purchase motivation?" (Lifestyle/safety necessity vs. single trusted brand).
X1.sample: 300 respondents (150 per arm) from 3 countries with high boat ownership (Norway, Sweden, Denmark). Recruit via panel providers to ensure demographic representation.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for the brand versus single brand arm. Secondary measure: proportion of respondents selecting "single trusted brand" vs. "lifestyle/safety necessity".

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average purchase intent score for the brand arm (lifestyle/safety necessity) than for the single brand arm.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average purchase intent score for the single brand arm than for the brand arm.

X1.decision_rule: If the brand arm’s average intent score is at least 5 points higher than the single brand arm, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (supporting T1). If the single brand arm’s score is at least 5 points higher, pursue a single‑brand consumer offering (supporting T2). If the difference is ≤ 5 points, do not expand.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes marine‑grade performance (durability, safety, and protection) rather than sustainability. Use Jotun’s existing brand credibility in marine coatings to justify premium pricing and sell through direct‑to‑consumer channels.

frame.objective: Determine whether Jotun should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its marine and protective coatings technology, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must assess demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer use case.
Evidence must be from sources read; cannot use later‑knowledge or financial data not in the dossier.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑focused product (e.g., outdoor gear, home protection) using marine‑grade coatings for a specific use case (e.g., waterproof clothing, marine‑grade paint for homes).
2) Expand into adjacent B2B segments (e.g., infrastructure, automotive, aerospace) using the same technology, rather than a consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing marine, protective, and powder coatings for shipyards, ship owners, and industry customers.
4) License the marine‑protective technology to third‑party manufacturers rather than building a direct consumer brand.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt waterproof clothing made from marine-grade coatings if they perceive it as high‑performance, durable, and safer than conventional waterproof materials, leading them to purchase it as a premium product.
T1.who_benefits: Jotun would benefit by capturing higher margins from a premium consumer brand, while consumers gain a product that promises superior protection and longevity.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from generic waterproof gear to marine‑grade products when they understand the underlying technology provides superior performance, safety, and durability, especially in harsh conditions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun would sell through its own retail website or partner channels at premium prices, leveraging its existing brand credibility in marine coatings to justify higher costs.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for performance claims.
Marine‑grade coatings are visible and communicable to end‑users.
Jotun can reach consumers through digital channels without significant distribution investment.
predictions: A survey of target consumers would show at least 40% indicating they would purchase marine‑grade waterproof clothing at a price 20% above conventional options.
Sales of a consumer‑brand product would be higher in regions where marine‑grade reputation is already established (e.g., Scandinavia).

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing consumer awareness of environmental impact drives purchase decisions; marine‑grade coatings are already associated with durability, so emphasizing sustainability adds a compelling reason to switch.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can price the product at a premium while leveraging its sustainability narrative, potentially capturing higher margins and building brand loyalty among environmentally conscious buyers.

predictions: A survey of target consumers would show at least 30% indicating they would purchase marine‑grade waterproof clothing primarily for sustainability reasons.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Performance vs Sustainability Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two versions of a product description for marine‑grade waterproof clothing. Participants see either a performance‑focused description emphasizing durability, safety, and marine‑grade technology, or a sustainability‑focused description emphasizing eco‑friendly materials, low environmental impact, and responsible sourcing. They are then asked to indicate willingness to pay a premium (20% above conventional price) and likelihood to purchase.
X1.sample: 500 adults in Scandinavia and Northern Europe, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self‑reported environmental concern (high, moderate, low).
X1.measure: Percentage of respondents who indicate willingness to pay the premium price; secondary measure: self‑reported primary purchase motivation (performance vs sustainability).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% will indicate willingness to pay the premium price; performance‑focused message will generate higher willingness than sustainability‑focused message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 30% will indicate willingness to pay the premium price; sustainability‑focused message will generate higher willingness than performance‑focused message.

X1.decision_rule: If willingness to pay the premium price is at least 40% for the performance version and at least 30% for the sustainability version, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing performance. If willingness is below 30% for either version, consider no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer motivations for performance or sustainability. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes marine‑grade performance (durability, safety, and protection) rather than sustainability. Use Jotun’s existing brand credibility in marine coatings to justify premium pricing and sell through direct‑to‑consumer channels.
final.target_customer: Outdoor enthusiasts, marine‑recovery enthusiasts, and homeowners in Scandinavia and Northern Europe who value high‑performance waterproof gear.
final.value_proposition: A premium‑priced waterproof clothing line made from marine‑grade coatings, marketed as the most durable and safe option available, leveraging Jotun’s proven marine coating technology.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 respondents, 8 weeks, €15,000) to measure willingness to pay a premium for performance‑focused messaging versus sustainability‑focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for marine‑grade waterproof clothing and whether consumers will actually pay a premium for performance claims remain uncertain. The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows willingness to pay the premium price below 30% for either messaging, or if sustainability messaging generates significantly higher willingness, we would reconsider the investment.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for eco‑friendly waterproof clothing, we would explore a sustainability‑focused proposition.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Marine vs. Home Protection Messaging
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with random assignment to either marine‑grade waterproof clothing or marine‑grade home protection messaging. Participants view product descriptions and are asked to indicate which they would purchase at a given price point and their willingness to pay.
X1.sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced between marine‑grade waterproof clothing and marine‑grade home protection messaging groups.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: choice frequency (percentage of participants selecting the assigned product). Secondary outcomes: average willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group assigned to marine‑grade waterproof clothing will show higher choice frequency and higher willingness to pay than group assigned to marine‑grade home protection messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group assigned to marine‑grade home protection messaging will show higher choice frequency and higher willingness to pay than group assigned to marine‑grade waterproof clothing.

X1.decision_rule: If the marine‑grade waterproof clothing group’s choice frequency exceeds the home protection group’s by at least 5 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 10% higher, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for waterproof clothing. If the home protection group’s choice frequency exceeds by at least 5 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 10% higher, develop a consumer proposition for home protection. If neither difference meets the thresholds, conclude no evidence justifies investment in either proposition at this time.

arguments.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with random assignment to either marine‑grade waterproof clothing or marine‑grade home protection messaging. Participants view product descriptions and are asked to indicate which they would purchase at a given price point and their willingness to pay.
arguments.sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced between marine‑grade waterproof clothing and marine‑grade home protection messaging groups.
arguments.measure: Primary outcome: choice frequency (percentage of participants selecting the assigned product). Secondary outcomes: average willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group assigned to marine‑grade waterproof clothing will show higher choice frequency and higher willingness to pay than group assigned to marine‑grade home protection messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group assigned to marine‑grade home protection messaging will show higher choice frequency and higher willingness to pay than group assigned to marine‑grade waterproof clothing.

arguments.decision_rule: If the marine‑grade waterproof clothing group’s choice frequency exceeds the home protection group’s by at least 5 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 10% higher, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for waterproof clothing. If the home protection group’s choice frequency exceeds by at least 5 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 10% higher, develop a consumer proposition for home protection. If neither difference meets the thresholds, conclude no evidence justifies investment in either proposition at this time.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Reason only from public sources knowable by 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week limit are analyst assumptions.
Must distinguish between current reach to individual buyers and potential demand.
Evidence must address consumer willingness to pay and actual purchase behavior, not just company claims.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing commercial/clinical offering without a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., deeper clinic/health‑club integration).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial/clinical markets.
4) License the technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than building a proprietary consumer line.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it provides a clear, actionable health message (e.g., 'body fat risk') and is marketed as a health tool, because they seek to reduce disease risk and are willing to pay for evidence-based results.
T1.who_benefits: Health-conscious consumers who view body fat as a risk factor for heart disease, diabetes and cancer.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They would change from relying on vague bathroom scales to a device that gives a numeric health risk, prompting purchase to monitor progress and reduce risk.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would capture value through premium pricing for a differentiated consumer product and repeat purchases of replacement sensors or accessories.
assumptions: Consumers in 1993 are aware of health risks of excess body fat and are motivated to reduce them.
A clear health message can be communicated effectively to home users.
Willingness to pay exceeds the cost of a basic home scale.
predictions: In a test offering a health-focused body-fat analyser, purchase intent will be higher than for a generic scale.
Surveyed buyers will cite health risk reduction as the primary reason for purchase.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: They would switch from manual bathroom scales to a device that provides an instant result, reducing the effort required to track progress and stay motivated.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would capture value through a low‑cost, easy‑to‑use consumer product sold at a price point below premium health devices, with potential for recurring sensor sales.
assumptions: Consumers in 1993 value convenience and simplicity in health monitoring.

Willingness to pay is lower for a simple device than for a health‑focused one.
predictions: In a test offering a one‑button body‑fat analyser, purchase intent will be higher than for a health‑focused device.

X1.name: Health‑focused vs convenience‑focused body‑fat analyser test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a health‑focused message: 'Measure your body fat risk and reduce heart disease, diabetes and cancer risk.' Group B sees a convenience‑focused message: 'Get an instant one‑button body‑fat measurement for quick health tracking.' Both groups see a price point (proposed €49.99) and a €9.99 sensor replacement option. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10) and primary reason (health risk vs convenience).
X1.sample: 400 US adults (200 per group), recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender and BMI.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary reason (health risk vs convenience).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and more participants citing health risk reduction as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and more participants citing convenience as the primary reason.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between the two groups is at least 1.5 points (e.g., Group A ≥ 6.5 and Group B ≤ 5.0), conclude the health‑focused proposition (T1) is more likely to succeed. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude the convenience‑focused proposition (T2) is more likely to succeed. If both groups are within 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.

final.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers who view body fat as a risk factor for heart disease, diabetes and cancer, and are willing to pay for evidence-based results.
final.value_proposition: A home body-fat analyser that provides a clear, numeric health risk message, enabling users to monitor progress and reduce disease risk, sold at a premium price point.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €18,000 online survey test (X1) to measure purchase intent and primary reason for a health‑focused versus convenience‑focused body‑fat analyser.
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay for a health‑focused device is unknown; the test will resolve this. Also uncertain is the relative strength of health‑risk versus convenience motivation.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 5% or no significant difference between health‑focused and convenience‑focused messages, the investment would be reconsidered.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Reason only from public sources knowable by 1993; no internal company data.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: The device provides real-time data, reducing uncertainty about weight changes and motivating consistent use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can charge a premium for a consumer line and sell directly to consumers, capturing value through higher margins than clinical sales.

predictions: Consumers will purchase a home body-fat analyser at a price above the clinical price point.

assumptions: Consumers prioritize ease of use over detailed accuracy.

predictions: Consumers will choose a device with a single button over a device requiring multiple steps.

X1.name: Consumer preference test: real-time vs. one-button messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a real-time health-monitoring message (continuous feedback) or a one-button measurement message (quick and easy). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 400 adults (200 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported health concern (high vs. low).
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) and maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Real-time message will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than one-button message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: One-button message will generate higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than real-time message.

X1.decision_rule: If the mean purchase intent for the real-time arm is at least 1.5 points higher than the one-button arm, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition based on real-time messaging. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, no expansion is recommended.

final.next_action: Execute the consumer preference test (real-time vs. one-button messaging) to determine whether real-time messaging yields higher purchase intent and willingness to pay. If the test supports T1, develop a consumer line; if not, reconsider
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay for a home body-fat analyser and the relative importance of real-time feedback versus convenience remain uncertain. The test will resolve this uncertainty.

X1.name: Home vs Fitness Messaging Test
X1.method: Online between‑subjects choice experiment with randomized exposure to either health‑focused or fitness‑focused messaging about a home body‑fat analyser.
X1.sample: 400 adults (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced by age, gender, and self‑reported health‑awareness (high vs low).
X1.measure: Purchase intent: binary choice to buy the device at a €199 price point; willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) in euros; self‑reported use intent (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health‑focused group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than fitness‑focused group, and overall purchase rate will be higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Fitness‑focused group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than health‑focused group, and overall purchase rate will be higher.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent of the health‑focused group exceeds that of the fitness‑focused group by at least 15 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for weight‑management. If the fitness‑focused group’s purchase intent exceeds health‑focused by at least 15 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant, proceed with a fitness‑focused proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.

revisions.reason: Simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns packing errors and does not address consumer demand, messaging, or purchase behavior for a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows that Tanita already has a strong commercial presence and a household scale is common, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand for a home body-fat analyser, nor willingness to pay a premium. The proposed test (X1) would resolve this uncertainty.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious home users who already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated home body‑fat analyser marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management, leveraging Tanita’s existing brand trust and retail distribution.
final.next_action: Run the proposed between‑subjects choice experiment (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under health‑focused versus fitness‑focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: Consumer demand for a home body‑fat analyser and willingness to pay a premium remain unproven. The test will clarify whether the health‑focused proposition generates sufficient demand.
would_change_if: If the test shows the fitness‑focused group’s purchase intent exceeds the health‑focused group by at least 15 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant, we would shift to a fitness‑focused proposition.
If neither condition is met, we would maintain the current position of not investing in a differentiated consumer proposition.

arguments.name: Home vs Fitness Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online between‑subjects choice experiment with randomized exposure to either health‑focused or fitness‑focused messaging about a home body‑fat analyser.
arguments.sample: 400 adults (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced by age, gender, and self‑reported health‑awareness (high vs low).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent: binary choice to buy the device at a €199 price point; willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) in euros; self‑reported use intent (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Health‑focused group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than fitness‑focused group, and overall purchase rate will be higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Fitness‑focused group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than health‑focused group, and overall purchase rate will be higher.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent of the health‑focused group exceeds that of the fitness‑focused group by at least 15 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for weight‑management. If the fitness‑focused group’s purchase intent exceeds health‑focused by at least 15 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant, proceed with a fitness‑focused proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows that Tanita already has a strong commercial presence and a household scale is common, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand for a home body-fat analyser, nor willingness to pay a premium. The test proposed (X1) would resolve this uncertainty.

The proposed test (X1) would resolve this uncertainty.
arguments.target_customer: Health‑conscious home users who already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data.
arguments.value_proposition: A differentiated home body‑fat analyser marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management, leveraging Tanita’s existing brand trust and retail distribution.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed between‑subjects choice experiment (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under health‑focused versus fitness‑focused messaging.
arguments.uncertainty: Consumer demand for a home body‑fat analyser and willingness to pay a premium remain unproven. The test will clarify whether the health‑focused proposition generates sufficient demand.
would_change_if: If the test shows the fitness‑focused group’s purchase intent exceeds the health‑focused group by at least 15 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant, we would shift to a fitness‑focused proposition.
If neither condition is met, we would maintain the current position of not investing in a differentiated consumer proposition.

This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Financial data is not in the dossier, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. The test budget of 20000 euros and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows consumers already use bathroom scales and keep track of body composition, but it does not show they would pay a premium for a home body-fat analyser or that they would purchase it for weight management. Conduct a small test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under health versus fitness messaging before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Reason only from public sources knowable by 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week limit are analyst assumptions.
Must distinguish between current reach to individual buyers and potential demand.
Evidence must address consumer willingness to pay and actual purchase behavior, not just company claims.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing commercial/clinical offering without a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., deeper clinic/health‑club integration).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial/clinical markets.
4) License the technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than building a proprietary consumer line.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management, because they already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data.
T1.who_benefits: Home users who want to track weight and body composition for health reasons.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If the device is positioned as a health tool, consumers will be motivated to purchase it for regular use rather than occasional use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value through premium pricing for a differentiated consumer product and repeat purchases of accessories or software updates.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides measurable health data.
Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits of body-fat measurement.
The device is accurate enough to be trusted by consumers for health decisions.
predictions: In a test market, consumers will purchase the device at a higher rate when marketed as a health monitoring tool compared to when marketed as a general weighing instrument.
Purchase intent will be higher among consumers who report concern about weight or health.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management, because they already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a fitness tracking tool for athletes and fitness enthusiasts, because they already use fitness equipment and seek performance metrics.
T2.who_benefits: Fitness enthusiasts and athletes who want to monitor body composition for training purposes.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If the device is positioned as a fitness tool, consumers will be motivated to purchase it for regular use to track progress and optimize training.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita can capture value through premium pricing for a fitness-focused consumer product and recurring revenue from accessories or subscription services.
assumptions: Fitness enthusiasts are willing to pay for a device that provides measurable body-fat data.
Marketing can effectively communicate the fitness benefits of body-fat measurement.
The device is accurate enough to be trusted for training decisions.
predictions: In a test market, consumers will purchase the device at a higher rate when marketed as a fitness tracking tool compared to when marketed as a health monitoring tool.
Purchase intent will be higher among consumers who report regular exercise or competition participation.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Health vs Fitness Messaging
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase decision.
X1.sample: 300 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported fitness interest (low, moderate, high).
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy"). 2) Willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. 3) Messaging preference (health vs fitness).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP when marketed as a health monitoring tool; purchase intent will be driven by health concern.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP when marketed as a fitness tracking tool; purchase intent will be driven by fitness interest.

X1.decision_rule: If the health messaging group achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and WTP ≥ €50, and the fitness messaging group achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and WTP ≥ €50, proceed with both propositions. If only one meets both thresholds, proceed with that proposition. If neither meets both, no expansion is justified.

revisions.reason: Simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns packing errors and does not address consumer purchase behavior, health versus fitness messaging, or willingness to pay. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows consumers already use bathroom scales and keep track of body composition, but it does not show they would pay a premium for a home body-fat analyser or that they would purchase it for weight management. Conduct a small test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under health versus fitness messaging before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Home users who already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data for weight management.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer product that provides accurate, health-focused body-fat measurement, marketed as a tool for tracking weight and overall health.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (health vs fitness messaging) to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the willingness to pay a premium for a home body-fat analyser are uncertain. The test will clarify whether consumers would adopt the device for weight management.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 40% or willingness to pay below €50, the investment would be reconsidered.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for fitness tracking or a clear willingness to pay premium, the recommendation would shift toward a fitness-focused proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, and identify what evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Reason only from public sources knowable by 1993; no internal company data.

Must distinguish between current reach to individual buyers and potential demand.
Evidence must address consumer willingness to pay and actual purchase behavior, not just company claims.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).

X1.name: Framed Messaging Choice Test
X1.method: Online survey with random assignment to one of two framing conditions. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=200). They are shown a description of a stand-on body-fat analyser with the same technical specifications, but the framing is different: Condition A frames the device as a health monitoring tool for weight management; Condition B frames it as a fitness tracking tool for athletes.
X1.sample: 200 adults (100 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported health interest.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: binary purchase intent (yes/no). Secondary: willingness to pay (EUR) and perceived accuracy importance.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition A.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two conditions is at least 15 percentage points (e.g., 40% in Condition A vs. 25% in Condition B), we conclude the framing aligns with the theory and recommend the corresponding consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 15 points, we conclude neither framing is significantly superior and recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns packing errors and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or purchase behavior for a home body-fat analyser. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows consumers already use bathroom scales and trust body-fat measurements as a health indicator, but it does not demonstrate willingness to pay a premium for a home body-fat analyser or that they will purchase it for weight management. The challenge test is pending.
final.target_customer: Home users who already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data for weight management.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions the device as a health monitoring tool for weight management, leveraging existing consumer scale adoption and the company’s medical evidence base.
final.next_action: Run the Framed Messaging Choice Test (or a similar willingness-to-pay experiment) to measure purchase intent differences between health‑framed and fitness‑framed messaging.
final.uncertainty: Willingness to pay a premium for a home body-fat analyser and actual purchase behavior are uncertain; the test results will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the challenge test shows a >=15 percentage‑point difference in purchase intent between health‑framed and fitness‑framed messaging, we would adopt the framing that aligns with the theory and recommend the corresponding consumer product.
If the test shows no significant difference or a smaller difference, we would conclude neither framing is significantly superior and recommend no expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available by late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources available by late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must assess demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer use case.
Must consider existing B2B products (shipping, aviation, military) and any gaps in individual buyer reach.
alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑focused product for a specific use case (e.g., marine safety for private boat owners).
2) Expand B2B offerings to new segments (e.g., commercial marine, aviation) without a consumer proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing shipping, aviation, and military markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer devices.
5) Partner with insurance or maritime authorities to embed the beacon in policies or safety programs.

T1.claim: Private boat owners will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz distress beacon because they perceive marine safety as a personal responsibility and a growing liability risk, leading them to purchase a device that provides real-time distress signals.
T1.who_benefits: Private boat owners and their owners/operators who face potential liability and safety costs.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from relying on manual distress signals (e.g., flare, radio call) to an automatic, satellite-linked beacon that can be activated from a smartphone or marine radio, reducing risk and perceived cost of an incident.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value through direct-to-consumer sales at a premium price, or through licensing the technology to marine equipment manufacturers for bundled safety packages.
assumptions: Liability insurance premiums for private boats will increase due to marine safety regulations.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides real-time distress signals.
Distribution channels (online, marine retailers) exist for consumer safety products.
predictions: Surveyed private boat owners will indicate intent to purchase a consumer beacon at a price above $100.
Pilot sales of a consumer beacon to boat owners will generate at least 500 units within 12 weeks.
Sales conversion will be driven by marketing on marine safety liability and real-time response benefits.

T2.claim: Insurance companies will require marine safety devices (e.g., 406 MHz beacons) as a condition of coverage for private boats, creating a demand for a consumer product that meets regulatory standards.
T2.who_benefits: Insurance providers seeking to mitigate claims costs and meet regulatory requirements.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from relying on voluntary marine safety equipment to mandating certified devices, forcing consumers to purchase compliant gear to maintain coverage.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value through licensing the technology to insurance underwriters and through premium-priced consumer devices sold directly or through marine retailers.

X1.name: Consumer vs Insurance-Driven Pilot
X1.method: Run a targeted online and in-person pilot in two segments: (1) private boat owners (targeted via marine forums and safety associations) and (2) insurance underwriters (via industry contacts). For both segments, offer a consumer-grade 406 MHz beacon at a premium price ($150) with a 12-week trial. Track purchase intent (willingness to pay) and actual sales conversion. For insurance underwriters, track whether they list the beacon as a required safety item for new policies.
X1.sample: Private boat owners: 200 targeted ads and 100 in-person offers in marine safety events. Insurance underwriters: 50 industry contacts and 20 policyholders. Total pilot: 250 participants.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (willingness to pay) and actual sales conversion for each segment.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Private boat owners will show purchase intent at least 20% and convert to at least 100 units within 12 weeks.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Insurance underwriters will list the beacon as a required safety item for at least 30% of new policies, and the pilot will achieve at least 200 sales with a conversion rate above 10%.

X1.decision_rule: If private boat owners achieve at least 100 units (20% of 500) and insurance underwriters list the beacon as required for at least 30% of new policies, proceed with a consumer proposition. If either segment fails to meet its threshold, reject the investment. If both meet their thresholds, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for private boat owners, leveraging the 406 MHz technology. Begin with a targeted pilot offering the beacon at a premium price ($150) to 200 boat owners, tracking purchase intent and sales conversion. If the pilot meets the 20% purchase intent and 100-unit threshold, proceed to broader consumer distribution; otherwise, reconsider the investment.
final.target_customer: Private boat owners and their owners/operators who face potential liability and safety costs.
final.value_proposition: A real-time, satellite-linked distress beacon that provides automatic emergency signals, reducing liability risk and the cost of a rescue operation.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 12-week pilot with 200 targeted offers, measuring purchase intent and actual sales conversion.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and willingness to pay a premium price for a marine safety device are uncertain. Insurance underwriting requirements and regulatory changes are also uncertain.
would_change_if: If the pilot fails to achieve the 20% purchase intent or 100-unit threshold, reconsider the investment.
If new evidence shows that insurance regulators are not requiring marine safety devices, T2 would become more likely and the investment would shift towards an insurance-driven model.
If consumer adoption is driven by other factors (e.g., marine safety awareness campaigns or partnerships with marine clubs), the strategy would need to be adjusted.

T1.claim: Private boat owners will purchase a consumer-grade 406 MHz distress beacon because they perceive marine safety as a personal responsibility and a growing fear of sinking or getting lost at sea.
T1.who_benefits: Individual boat owners and their families who value peace of mind and legal compliance.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Increased awareness of marine risks and potential sinking incidents creates a perceived need for a reliable emergency signal; the beacon offers a low-cost, easy-to-use solution that meets this need.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon directly to consumers at a premium price, leveraging its existing distribution channels and brand reputation for reliability.
assumptions: Boats owned by private individuals are a significant market.
The fear of sinking and getting lost is a growing concern for boat owners.
The 406 MHz beacon is perceived as a reliable and effective emergency signal.
predictions: Surveyed private boat owners will express intent to purchase a consumer beacon at a price they find acceptable.
Sales of a consumer beacon will be higher in regions with higher boat ownership rates.
Willingness to pay will be higher for a beacon marketed as a personal safety device rather than a professional tool.
T1.first_claim: Private boat owners will purchase a consumer-grade 406 MHz distress beacon because they perceive marine safety as a personal responsibility and a growing fear of sinking or getting lost at sea.

T2.claim: Insurance companies and maritime authorities will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz distress beacon as part of safety programs because it reduces claims costs and enhances public safety, creating a demand for a reliable emergency signal.
T2.who_benefits: Insurance companies seeking to lower liability costs and maritime authorities aiming to improve safety compliance.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Regulatory pressure and the financial impact of claims make it cost-effective for insurers and authorities to provide a proven emergency signal; the beacon offers a low-cost, reliable solution that meets compliance requirements.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell the beacon through insurance brokers and safety program providers at volume prices, capturing recurring revenue from sales and licensing.
assumptions: Insurance companies are willing to fund safety devices that reduce claims.
Maritime authorities have the authority and resources to promote the use of beacons.
The beacon is certified and recognized as a compliant emergency signal.
predictions: Insurance companies will express interest in purchasing beacons for their policyholders.
Maritime authorities will allocate funding for beacon distribution in safety programs.
Sales will be driven by volume contracts rather than individual consumer purchases.

X1.name: Consumer vs. Insurance Demand Test
X1.method: Online survey with two parallel arms: Arm A targets individual boat owners (recruited via marine forums and boat clubs) and Arm B targets insurance brokers and maritime safety program providers. Each participant sees a product description of the 406 MHz beacon and is asked to indicate willingness to purchase (price range) and likelihood to purchase (1-7).
X1.sample: 200 participants: 100 boat owners (private boat owners) and 100 insurance brokers/safety program providers, recruited via targeted online panels.
X1.measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (1-7) for the consumer beacon.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Boat owners in Arm A will show higher WTP and purchase intent than brokers in Arm B, because they perceive marine safety as a personal responsibility.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Brokers in Arm B will show higher WTP and purchase intent than boat owners in Arm A, because they seek cost-effective safety solutions for their clients.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for boat owners in Arm A exceeds brokers in Arm B by at least 15 points (e.g., 60 vs. 45 on a 1-7 scale) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), we conclude T1 is more likely. If brokers in Arm B exceed boat owners in Arm A by at least 15 points, we conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than 15 points or not statistically significant, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend further market research.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for private boat owners, leveraging ACR’s existing 406 MHz beacon technology and distribution channels. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: Private boat owners and their families who value peace of mind and legal compliance in marine safety.
final.value_proposition: A reliable, low-cost 406 MHz distress beacon marketed as a personal safety device, offering peace of mind and compliance for boating activities.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs. Insurance Demand Test (Arm A: boat owners; Arm B: brokers/safety providers) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent, and apply the decision rule to decide whether to proceed.
final.uncertainty: The size of the private boat owner market and their actual willingness to pay for a consumer beacon remain uncertain. Evidence from 2002 shows the beacon is approved for public use but does not demonstrate consumer demand.
would_change_if: If the test shows boat owners’ willingness to pay is significantly lower than brokers’, or if the difference is not statistically significant, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and explore alternative B2B or licensing options.
If new evidence from 2002 shows a large, untapped consumer market or strong insurance demand, we would revise the recommendation to prioritize that segment.

Each group sees a product description of a 406 MHz PLB priced at $150-$200, marketed either as a marine safety necessity (T1) or as a compliance requirement for insurance policies (T2). Both groups are asked about purchase intent (1-7 scale) and willingness to pay a premium.
X1.sample: 400 respondents: 200 private boat owners (recruited via marine forums and boat clubs) and 200 insurance professionals (recruited via industry associations). Stratify by region (Florida, California, Texas) to reflect boat ownership and insurance penetration.

final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Insurance Messaging Test (400 respondents, 10-week online survey) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: Consumer demand and price sensitivity are unknown; insurance demand is uncertain. The test will resolve whether a consumer proposition is viable.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts, leveraging ACR's existing 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and price sensitivity before full-scale rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available by late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources available by late 2002; no internal company data.
Investment decision must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, market opportunity, or competitive advantage.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must consider current consumer reach of ACR Electronics and potential new customer segments.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., marine safety for private boat owners).
2) Expand into a broader consumer market without a specific use case, leveraging the distress-beacon technology for general emergency communication.
3) Maintain current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion).
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third-party manufacturers for consumer devices rather than building a proprietary consumer product.

T1.claim: Private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they currently lack reliable, affordable emergency communication tools and would pay a premium for a device that reliably sends a distress signal via 406 MHz satellite, reducing their risk of being stranded or unreachable.
T1.who_benefits: Private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts who face extended isolation at sea or in remote areas.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They currently rely on traditional PLBs or cell phones, which may not reach a satellite or fail in emergencies, and they perceive the risk of being unreachable as high enough to justify a purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by selling a premium, differentiated product through retail and marine safety channels, leveraging its existing certification and brand credibility in emergency equipment.
assumptions: There is a meaningful segment of private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts willing to pay for a satellite distress beacon.
The 406 MHz technology is reliable and interoperable with existing emergency systems.
ACR can reach this segment through existing distribution channels or new retail partnerships.
predictions: Surveyed boat owners will indicate high intent to purchase a satellite distress beacon if priced within $100-$150.
Pilot sales of a consumer product will generate at least 100 units in the first 12 weeks, indicating measurable demand.
T1.first_claim: Private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they currently lack reliable, affordable emergency communication tools and would pay a premium for a device that reliably sends a distress signal via 406 MHz satellite, reducing their risk of being stranded or unreachable.

T2.claim: ACR's existing B2B customers (military and commercial marine users) will adopt a consumer proposition because they already trust ACR's emergency equipment and are willing to pay for a reliable, certified device that meets their safety requirements.
T2.who_benefits: ACR's current B2B customers who need reliable emergency communication for ships and aircraft.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: These customers already use ACR's products and are comfortable with certification and performance; they will extend that trust to a consumer product if it meets their safety standards.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can capture value by leveraging its existing brand credibility and certification to sell a consumer product at a premium price, using the same distribution channels it uses for B2B sales.
assumptions: ACR's B2B customers are willing to recommend or purchase a consumer product.
The consumer product will meet the same safety and performance standards expected by ACR's B2B customers.
ACR can reach B2B customers through existing channels and maintain brand trust.
predictions: B2B customers will indicate high intent to purchase a consumer product if priced within $150-$200.
Pilot sales of a consumer product will generate at least 50 units from B2B customers in the first 12 weeks, indicating measurable demand from existing customers.
T2.first_claim: ACR's existing B2B customers (military and commercial marine users) will adopt a consumer proposition because they already trust ACR's emergency equipment and are willing to pay for a reliable, certified device that meets their safety requirements.

X1.name: Channel-Specific Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offers and price ranges, segmented by target audience (private boat owners vs. B2B customers). Participants view a product description and are asked to indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay. Recruitment is limited to U.S. and U.K. residents with boat ownership or commercial marine interest.
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 private boat owners/Outdoor enthusiasts (recruited via marine forums and outdoor groups) and 150 B2B decision-makers (recruited via trade associations and industry contacts).
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of respondents saying "yes" when offered a $100-$150 price point) and maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Private boat owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than B2B customers across all price points.
prediction_by_theory.T2: B2B customers will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than private boat owners across all price points.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for private boat owners exceeds that for B2B customers by at least 10 percentage points across all price points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting private boat owners. If purchase intent for B2B customers exceeds that for private boat owners by at least 10 percentage points across all price points, pursue a B2B-focused consumer proposition. If neither segment meets the 10-point threshold, do not invest in a consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence about a label printer reducing packing errors does not address consumer demand for a satellite distress beacon, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts, leveraging ACR’s existing 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and price sensitivity before full-scale rollout.
final.target_customer: Private boat owners and outdoor enthusiasts who face extended isolation at sea or in remote areas and currently lack reliable, affordable emergency communication tools.
final.value_proposition: A premium, differentiated consumer product that reliably sends a distress signal via 406 MHz satellite, reducing the risk of being stranded or unreachable, while leveraging ACR’s existing certification and brand credibility.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Channel-Specific Purchase Intent Test (300 respondents, 10‑week pilot) to measure purchase intent and price willingness for private boat owners versus B2B customers.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and willingness to pay for a satellite distress beacon are uncertain. Evidence from 2002 shows ACR already had B2B customers and a product approved by the FCC, but no source shows consumer demand or price
would_change_if: If the pilot shows purchase intent for private boat owners is at least 10 percentage points lower than for B2B customers across all price points, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and focus on B2B expansion.
If new evidence from 2002 shows a large, existing consumer market for marine safety devices or that ACR already had retail distribution, we would reassess the investment case.

arguments.method: Online survey with two parallel paths: Path A targets private boat owners (n=200) with a consumer‑focused PLB proposition. Path B targets marine insurance brokers (n=100) with a B2B‑focused PLB proposition. Both paths present the same product description, price, and purchase intent questions (e.g., “How likely are you to purchase this PLB for a private boat?” on a 7‑point scale).
arguments.sample: Path A: 200 U.S. private boat owners (estimated 200,000 owners in the U.S.). Path B: 100 marine insurance brokers (estimated 100 in key marine regions).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Private boat owners will report higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than brokers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Brokers will report higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than private boat owners.

arguments.decision_rule: If Path A purchase intent ≥ 5.0 and Path B purchase intent ≤ 3.0, conclude T1 is supported. If Path B purchase intent ≥ 5.0 and Path A purchase intent ≤ 3.0, conclude T2 is supported. If both thresholds are met, conclude both theories are supported. If neither threshold is met, conclude neither theory is supported.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 400 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced across regions with small garden ownership (east coast) and large farm regions (Midwest).
X1.measure: 1) WTP for a differentiated lawn tractor marketed as a single-use tool (T1) vs a versatile tool (T2). 2) Intent to purchase (binary: "Would buy" vs "Would not buy").

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP for the single-use proposition will be higher than for the versatile proposition in small garden regions.
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP for the versatile proposition will be higher than for the single-use proposition in small garden regions.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for the single-use proposition in small garden regions exceeds the average WTP for the versatile proposition by at least 10% (e.g., €200 vs €180), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the opposite difference holds, pursue a versatile proposition. If the difference is below 10%, do not commit to a differentiated proposition and consider other alternatives.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959 and sales rose 76% in 1960-1979, but it does not show household demand for a single-use lawn tractor. Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent before investing.
final.target_customer: Households with small gardens who need a quick, one-time chore solution
final.value_proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor marketed as a convenient, single-use tool for small gardens, sold through independent dealers at a premium price.
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Proposition Preference Test (400 households, 6 weeks, €18,000) to compare willingness-to-pay for single-use vs versatile propositions.
final.uncertainty: Whether households in 1962 actually need a dedicated lawn tractor for small gardens and are willing to pay a premium for it.
would_change_if: If the test shows the versatile proposition (T2) has higher willingness-to-pay in small garden regions, we would shift to a multi-functional proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference or lower willingness-to-pay for the single-use proposition, we would reconsider the investment or pursue other alternatives.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small garden chores, leveraging Deere’s existing tractor engineering and independent dealer network. Begin with a limited launch of a dedicated lawn tractor model, marketed as a convenient, single-use tool for small gardens.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-1962
No access to internal company data or financial figures
Test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeframe for any proposed experiment
Must consider the existing distribution network of independent dealers and the current reach to individual buyers
alternatives: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small-scale landscaping, gardening, or light construction)

T1.claim: Households will adopt a lawn tractor if it is marketed as a convenient, single-use tool for small gardens, because the task is too small for a farm tractor and too small for a garden tool, so a differentiated consumer proposition captures a new segment.
T1.who_benefits: Households with small gardens who need a quick, one-time chore
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They currently use a shovel or push mower for small jobs; a dedicated lawn tractor removes the need to switch tools and reduces chores.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells a differentiated model through independent dealers at a premium price, capturing margin on a new consumer segment.
assumptions: Households in 1962 have small gardens and need a quick chore solution
Independent dealers can reach these households
Marketing can differentiate the product from existing garden tools
predictions: Surveyed households will indicate willingness to purchase a dedicated lawn tractor for small gardens
Sales of a differentiated model will be higher in regions with small garden ownership than in large farm regions
T1.first_claim: Households will adopt a lawn tractor if it is marketed as a convenient, single-use tool for small gardens, because the task is too small for a farm tractor and too small for a garden tool, so a differentiated consumer proposition captures a new segment.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: They currently use a shovel, push mower, and hand tools for small jobs; a single, versatile lawn tractor reduces tool switching and chores.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells a differentiated model through independent dealers at a premium price, capturing margin on a multi-functional product.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Single vs Multi-Use Lawn Tractor
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants see a description of a lawn tractor and are asked: (1) Would you buy a dedicated lawn tractor for small garden chores? (2) Would you buy a versatile lawn tractor that can mow, weed, and light cleanup? (3) Would you buy either version? They also indicate maximum willingness to pay (EUR).
X1.sample: 400 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced for garden ownership (small vs large) and region (urban vs rural).
X1.measure: 1) Percentage choosing dedicated lawn tractor. 2) Percentage choosing versatile lawn tractor. 3) Difference in choice between the two groups. 4) Maximum willingness to pay for each option.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Versatile lawn tractor will be chosen by ≥60% of households; dedicated lawn tractor by <20%.

final.target_customer: Households with small gardens who need a quick, one-time chore solution.
final.value_proposition: A dedicated lawn tractor that removes the need to switch tools, offering convenience and efficiency for small garden tasks.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test to validate demand for a dedicated lawn tractor versus a versatile lawn tractor.
final.uncertainty: The actual demand for a differentiated consumer proposition is uncertain; the test will determine whether households will choose a dedicated lawn tractor over a versatile one.
would_change_if: If the test shows the versatile lawn tractor share ≥60% and the dedicated share <20%, we would shift focus to a multi-use proposition.
If the test shows both shares <20%, we would conclude inconclusive demand and reconsider the investment.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and choice-based conjoint analysis.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners (aged 25-55) recruited via panel, balanced across urban, suburban, and rural demographics.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay (WTP) for a branded lawn tractor (T1) versus a specialized lawn mower (T2).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent for the branded lawn tractor will be at least 15% higher than for a generic tractor, and WTP will be at least 20% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for the specialized lawn mower will be at least 15% higher than for a generic mower, and WTP will be at least 20% higher.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for the branded lawn tractor exceeds the generic tractor by ≥15% and WTP exceeds the generic tractor by ≥20%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping. If purchase intent for the specialized mower exceeds the generic mower by ≥15% and WTP exceeds the generic mower by ≥20%, develop a specialized lawn mower line. If neither condition is met, maintain current business model.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping, leveraging Deere's existing tractor engineering and independent dealer network. Begin with a limited pilot offering a branded lawn tractor at a 20% premium over a generic equivalent to test household demand and capture value.
final.target_customer: Individual homeowners and small garden owners who need a tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.
final.value_proposition: A branded, differentiated lawn tractor that combines Deere's engineering reputation with a consumer-friendly design, sold through independent dealers at a premium price to capture margin.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (500 homeowners, 10 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the branded lawn tractor versus a generic tractor.
final.uncertainty: The size of the household market for small-scale landscaping in 1962 is unknown; independent dealer willingness to promote a differentiated product is uncertain; the premium price point is unproven.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the branded lawn tractor is below 15% or willingness to pay is below 20% of a generic tractor, we would abandon the differentiated proposition and maintain the current business model.
If new evidence shows strong demand for a specialized lawn mower (e.g., mowing as a recurring task) and independent dealers are willing to promote it, we would shift focus to a specialized line.
If financial data revealed Deere's ability to achieve a 20% margin on a differentiated product, the investment case would strengthen.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test for Lawn Tractor Use Case
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario
X1.sample: 500 U.S. households recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and garden size (small vs. large).
X1.measure: 1) Choice: prefer a single-use lawn tractor for a specific garden chore (T1) or a versatile lawn tractor for multiple tasks (T2). 2) Willingness to pay: maximum price they would pay for each option. 3) Purchase intent: would buy the product if price was met.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Households will choose the single-use lawn tractor for a specific chore and show higher willingness to pay for that option, indicating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Households will choose the versatile lawn tractor for multiple tasks and show higher willingness to pay for that option, indicating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition focused on versatility.

X1.decision_rule: If the single-use lawn tractor receives at least 55% of choices and at least 55% of respondents indicate willingness to pay at least $1,500, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case. If the versatile lawn tractor receives at least 55% of choices and at least 55% of respondents indicate willingness to pay at least $1,500, develop a differentiated consumer proposition for multiple tasks. If neither meets the thresholds, do not invest.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for a single-use lawn tractor. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959 and sales rose 76% in 1960-1979, but it does not show households will purchase a single-use lawn tractor or that it meets a specific use case. Run the proposed consumer preference test to measure demand for a single-use lawn tractor before committing resources.

final.value_proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor marketed as a convenient, single-use tool for small garden chores, sold through independent dealers at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (500 households, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure choice and willingness to pay for a single-use lawn tractor versus a versatile lawn tractor.
final.uncertainty: Demand for a single-use lawn tractor is unknown; the test will resolve this. Also uncertain is whether households will pay a premium price and whether independent dealers can effectively reach these households.
would_change_if: If the test shows the versatile lawn tractor receives at least 55% of choices and willingness to pay meets the threshold, we would shift to a differentiated proposition for multiple tasks.
If the test shows neither option meets the thresholds, we would maintain the current business model with no expansion.

X1.name: Messaging Test: Convenience vs Status
X1.method: Recruit households with small gardens (n=200) and randomly assign them to one of two groups. Group A receives a message emphasizing convenience and single-machine convenience (e.g., 'One tool for mowing, leaf blowing, and more'). Group B receives a message emphasizing status and capability (e.g., 'Show off your wealth with a premium lawn tractor'). Both groups are shown a price point and a call to book a test drive. Track units booked per household.
X1.sample: 200 households with small gardens, recruited via a national panel, balanced by income and region.
X1.measure: Number of households booking a test drive in each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will book more test drives than Group B (convenience message dominates).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will book more test drives than Group A (status message dominates).

X1.decision_rule: If Group A books at least 30% more units than Group B, adopt the convenience proposition. If Group B books at least 30% more units than Group A, adopt the status proposition. If the difference is <10% points, do not commit to either message and consider both.

final.next_action: Run the proposed messaging test (Convenience vs Status) with 200 households to measure test-drive bookings and decide on the message.
final.uncertainty: The actual purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated unit are unknown. The test will resolve whether convenience or status drives adoption.
would_change_if: If the test shows Group B (status message) booking at least 30% more units than Group A, we would shift to a status-driven proposition.
If neither group shows a meaningful difference (<10% points), we would consider both messages and not commit to either.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for lawn tractors in 1962, we would reconsider the investment.

X1.name: Branded vs. Generic Lawn Tractor Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a branded lawn tractor (with Deere branding and differentiated features) or a generic lawn tractor (no branding, generic specification). Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners with small gardens (estimated 5,000 respondents). Each participant sees one ad for 12 weeks, and after exposure, they are asked: “Would you be interested in purchasing this product?" and “Would you be willing to pay a 20% premium over a generic equivalent?"
X1.sample: 5,000 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region. Randomly assigned 2,500 to see branded ad, 2,500 to see generic ad.
X1.measure: Primary measure: binary purchase intent (yes/no). Secondary measure: premium willingness (percentage willing to pay at least 20% more).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Branded ad group will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than generic ad group, and premium willingness will be at least 5% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Generic ad group will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than branded ad group, and premium willingness will be at least 5% higher.

X1.decision_rule: If branded group purchase intent ≥ 15% and premium willingness ≥ 5% → proceed to develop differentiated consumer proposition (support T1). If generic group purchase intent ≥ 15% and premium willingness ≥ 5% → consider expanding dealer network without differentiation (support T2). If neither meets threshold → maintain current model.

arguments.name: Branded vs. Generic Lawn Tractor Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a branded lawn tractor (with Deere branding and differentiated features) or a generic lawn tractor (no branding, generic specification). Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners with small gardens (estimated 5,000 respondents). Each participant sees one ad for 12 weeks, and after exposure, they are asked: “Would you be interested in purchasing this product?" and “Would you be willing to pay a 20% premium over a generic equivalent?"
arguments.sample: 5,000 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region. Randomly assigned 2,500 to see branded ad, 2,500 to see generic ad.
arguments.measure: Primary measure: binary purchase intent (yes/no). Secondary measure: premium willingness (percentage willing to pay at least 20% more).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Branded ad group will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than generic ad group, and premium willingness will be at least 5% higher.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Generic ad group will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than branded ad group, and premium willingness will be at least 5% higher.

arguments.decision_rule: If branded group purchase intent ≥ 15% and premium willingness ≥ 5% → proceed to develop differentiated consumer proposition (support T1). If generic group purchase intent ≥ 15% and premium willingness ≥ 5% → consider expanding dealer network without differentiation (support T2). If neither meets threshold → maintain current model.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows Deere had a prototype lawn tractor built in 1959 and began production in 1963, but it does not demonstrate household demand for a branded unit or that Deere can capture value at a premium. arguments.target_customer: Individual homeowners and small garden owners who need a tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.
arguments.value_proposition: A branded, differentiated lawn tractor that leverages Deere's engineering reputation and independent dealer distribution to offer a premium-priced, specialized product for small-scale tasks.
arguments.next_action: Conduct the proposed Branded vs. Generic Lawn Tractor Test (12-week, €12,000) to measure purchase intent and premium willingness before committing to a differentiated proposition.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the household market, the willingness to pay a premium, and the ability of independent dealers to promote a differentiated product are uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 15% or premium willingness below 5% for the branded unit, the recommendation would shift to maintain the current model.
